passage: The residents' meeting in the laundry room of the Dublin block ran forty minutes before Nkechi understood how it worked: two neighbours, Mr. Doyle and Mrs. Kearney, spoke to each other while the rest looked at their shoes. Ingrid, from the top floor, opened her mouth twice and closed it again. Nkechi, twenty years old, had come only because the notice was under the door. Then Nkechi raised a hand. "Is there a written agenda? And are the bin rules written down anywhere?" A pause. Mr. Doyle said there had never been. "Could we make one, and could everyone say one thing they need?" Ingrid murmured, "Actually, the lift..." and the room turned to listen.

qa.q: Which two neighbours did most of the talking?
qa.a: Mr. Doyle and Mrs. Kearney spoke to each other.

qa.q: How did Nkechi feel about the way the meeting worked, and why speak up?
qa.a: Nkechi felt concerned that it was unfair, with two neighbours running everything while others stayed silent, so Nkechi asked for written rules and a turn for everyone.

qa.q: What could Nkechi do after this meeting to keep it fair?
qa.a: Help write the agenda and rules down and invite every resident to name one need.

qa.q: What might Ingrid have been feeling before the room turned to listen?
qa.a: Hesitant and unsure, wanting to speak about the lift but afraid to interrupt; opening and closing the mouth shows it.

grounding: A young resident notices a few people dominating a meeting and asks for written rules and turns to speak.

passage: Forty residents sat on plastic chairs in the society clubhouse, but only about four voices were heard. Gurpreet, a new tenant of twenty, watched the treasurer and a retired colonel argue about generator charges for half an hour. Jatin, from B wing, sat with folded arms, tapping a pen but never speaking. Nobody had seen the by-laws. At the end, Gurpreet went up to the secretary and asked, "Can I get a copy of the rules, please, and the last meeting's minutes?" Then, to the room, "Jatin, it looked like you had a point about parking?" Jatin blinked, then nodded. The secretary promised copies by Sunday, and next time the turns to speak would be written on the board.

qa.q: How many residents sat in the clubhouse?
qa.a: Forty residents sat on plastic chairs in the clubhouse.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet have felt watching Jatin, and why ask Jatin directly?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt concerned for the quiet resident after noticing the silent pen-tapping, and wanted Jatin to have a chance to speak.

qa.q: Which request by Gurpreet helped the society work better for all?
qa.a: Asking for the rules and the minutes in writing, and for turns to speak on the board.

qa.q: What is it like for Jatin sitting silent while others argue?
qa.a: Frustrating and unheard, with a point about parking but no obvious space to share it, until someone asks.

grounding: A young resident sees a few people dominate a society meeting and asks for written rules and fair turns.

passage:
Hi Sachin,
You asked about our society meeting. It was strange. About forty people came to the clubhouse, but only three spoke the whole two hours: the secretary, his brother-in-law and a man who owns four flats. They decided the lift repair, the watchman's hours and a new rule banning tenants from the pool, all in about ten minutes. The tenants sat at the back and stared at their phones. One aunty raised her hand twice and they spoke over her both times.
I almost left. Then I stood up, voice wobbling, and asked if we could have the rules and the minutes in writing before anything was voted on. It went very quiet. Then an old gentleman at the back clapped.
They agreed to circulate the minutes. I'll believe it when I see them.
Kamal

qa.q: How many people spoke during the whole meeting?
qa.a: Only three spoke the whole two hours.

qa.q: How did Kamal feel when standing up to ask for written rules?
qa.a: Kamal was nervous, with a wobbling voice, but determined enough to speak because the meeting felt unfair.

qa.q: What else could Kamal do to keep the meeting fair next time?
qa.a: Kamal could come again, sit with the quieter residents and support the aunty when she raises her hand, so more voices are heard.

qa.q: What would it be like for the aunty whose hand was ignored?
qa.a: She probably felt dismissed and small, and may stop trying to speak unless someone else backs her up.

grounding: It illustrates a young resident noticing that a few people dominate a society meeting and asking for written rules.

passage: Thanks, Himani, for having me on the campus podcast. So, I'm Hrithik, twenty-one, and the story is about my building. I started going to society meetings because my parents were travelling. First meeting, I just watched. Two uncles in the front row, same two every time, finished each other's sentences. Everyone else nodded or looked at the ceiling. One of them said, "It's always been this way," about a parking fee nobody had seen written down. And I noticed the ladies from the B-wing sitting completely silent. Later, one of them told me in the lift she'd tried once and been laughed at. So at the next meeting I asked, politely, for a copy of the bye-laws and a speaking list. The uncles were annoyed. But now the B-wing aunties speak. It's slower, messier, and much better.

qa.q: What did one of the front-row men say about the parking fee?
qa.a: He said, "It's always been this way."

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling at the first meeting, and what shows it?
qa.a: Hrithik was uneasy and curious, quietly watching who spoke and noticing that the B-wing ladies stayed silent.

qa.q: Which steps worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking politely for the bye-laws and a speaking list moved power away from a couple of loud voices and gave quieter residents a fair turn.

qa.q: How might the lady in the lift have felt about the meetings before the speaking list?
qa.a: She probably felt humiliated after being laughed at and unwilling to try again, so the list may have made her feel safer to speak.

grounding: It illustrates a young resident noticing that a few people dominate the society meetings while others stay silent, and asking for written rules and fair turns.

passage: I'm Ishita, and I sat three rows behind Asif uncle at the Green Park residents' meeting last month. I'll tell you what I saw, though I can't know what he was thinking. The committee chair talked for forty minutes about painting the gate. When the water shortage came up, Asif uncle raised his hand. The chair said, "Later," and moved on. Asif uncle lowered his hand and stared at his knees. He rubbed his thumb over a folded paper, what looked like a list of complaints from the old block. At the end, people rushed out. I went up to him and said, "Can I read your list?" He smiled, a little surprised. The next week I typed it up, and we both asked the committee, in writing, for water to be the first item. It was.

qa.q: What topic did the chair talk about for forty minutes?
qa.a: Painting the gate.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling when watching Asif uncle lower his hand?
qa.a: Ishita seems uncomfortable and concerned, noticing his lowered hand and the folded paper and choosing to go up to him afterwards.

qa.q: Why did putting the request in writing help?
qa.a: A written request is harder to wave away with "later", and it made the water shortage a fixed item that the whole committee had to address.

qa.q: How might Asif uncle have experienced being told "Later"?
qa.a: He may have felt brushed aside and discouraged after preparing a list, and then surprised and grateful when someone younger took an interest.

grounding: It illustrates a young resident noticing that the chair dominates a meeting while another resident is silenced, and helping bring the issue in writing.

passage:
First Sunday. Karthik went to his first residents' association meeting because the lift had been broken for three weeks. Two retired men did all the talking; everyone else stared at their phones. When Yamini from 3B tried to speak about the lift, the treasurer said, "Next agenda," and she sat down.
Second Sunday. Karthik came early, with Yamini and three others from the upper floors. He had printed the association's own by-laws. "Sir, clause 6 says any member can add an agenda item in writing. Here is ours: the lift, with quotes from two repair firms." The room went quiet. The treasurer frowned, then read the paper.
Fourth Sunday. The lift was working. At the meeting, Karthik noticed three people who had never spoken before raise their hands. The chairman now kept a list of speakers on the whiteboard.

qa.q: Which clause did Karthik point to?
qa.a: Clause 6, which says any member can add an agenda item in writing.

qa.q: What might Karthik have felt at the first meeting when Yamini was cut off?
qa.a: Karthik probably felt frustrated and uneasy at how two men dominated and a neighbour was silenced.

qa.q: Which of Karthik's steps changed how the meetings worked?
qa.a: Showing up with neighbours, bringing the written by-laws, and adding a clear agenda item with repair quotes.

qa.q: How might Yamini have felt at the second meeting?
qa.a: Yamini probably felt supported and less alone, since her lift concern was finally heard with others backing her.

grounding: It illustrates a young resident who notices a few people dominating a housing society meeting and helps it work for all by showing up, using written rules and speaking fairly.
